sources.news_title: Stellantis signs deal with Roshel to sell idled Brampton, Ont. assembly plant
sources.text:
Stellantis signs deal with Roshel to sell idled Brampton, Ont. assembly plant
							November 12, 2026 
							
By The Canadian Press
								
							
						
The companies said in a joint news release they are also exploring future collaboration opportunities across vehicle technologies and related services in the defence industry
Talking Points
Stellantis has signed an agreement to sell its idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel. The asset purchase agreement includes the facility and equipment, with plans for future collaboration in vehicle technologies. This sale occurs amid stalled contract negotiations between Stellantis and the union representing over 9,000 workers, who recently authorized a potential strike.
- More than 2,000 workers were laid off when the Brampton plant halted operations in 2023.
- The sale could allow 700 to 1,000 laid-off employees to return to work under Roshel.
- Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown urges Stellantis to resolve issues with Unifor and repay taxpayer funding.
This development raises concerns about job security and the future of Canada's automotive industry, as the federal government seeks to ensure commitments made by Stellantis are upheld.
Nov. 10, 2026, Brampton, Ont. — Stellantis says it has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its idled Brampton, Ont. assembly plant.
Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the facility and associated equipment from the automaker for an undisclosed amount.
The companies said in a joint news release they are also exploring future collaboration opportunities across vehicle technologies and related services in the defence industry.
The move comes as contract talks between Stellantis and the union representing more than 9,000 of its workers in Canada remain at an impasse.
The two sides have clashed over the future of the Brampton site, as well as issues around job security. Last month, Stellantis workers in Canada voted to give their union a mandate to strike, with 97.3 per cent of members in favour of authorizing a potential job action.
“We’re currently not in a strike position, and obviously, lots of this [is] to be worked out. Our goal here is to reach a resolution and to get to the bargaining table when we can, and we’ll do our best to get an agreement,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said at a press conference Monday evening.
“A strike is always a last resort, and it remains a last resort here.”
She said the union will evaluate its next move and that it has a “four-party meeting” scheduled for later in the week, with the company and government officials to discuss the future of the Brampton plant.
Payne said the sale of an auto assembly plant and loss of vehicle production capacity is devastating for Canada’s industry.
“Having sold an auto plant is a worst-case scenario, and that’s what we’re facing right now. Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers,” she said.
“Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of our national auto strategy and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect autoworkers from this U.S. trade war.”
Talks broke down in September, when Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel, a Brampton-based manufacturer of armoured vehicles, for a potential sale of the facility.
More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.
The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.
“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” said Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa in the news release.
“With this announcement, we are driving forward our broader strategic goals, opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry, and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”
Roshel founder and CEO Roman Shimonov said the company’s plan is to create a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, “which will allow Canadian companies to better serve customers at home and export into allied markets.
“Aligned with Canada’s defence industrial strategy, it will strengthen our sovereign industrial capabilities, drive local economic growth and bring much-needed manufacturing space and jobs to the Toronto area,” Shimonov said in the release.
“We look forward to working collaboratively with government and the broader community to bring this vision to life.”
As the facility returns to operations, there will be opportunities for around 700-to-1,000 laid-off Stellantis employees to return to work under Roshel. The defence company also plans to lease around one-quarter of the site’s space back to Stellantis for automotive work.
The transaction is expected to close by the end of this year, subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.
Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown said in a statement Monday that he welcomes the opportunity for a local company to bring manufacturing back to the location.
He said Unifor members also deserve a fair resolution from Stellantis.
“I’m calling on Stellantis to work with Unifor to reach that resolution, and on Roshel to work directly with Local 1285 to identify hiring and training opportunities for laid-off Brampton autoworkers,” he said.
Brown said Stellantis also needs to repay taxpayers for the public funding it received to support automotive production in Brampton.
“I will continue pressing the federal government to recover that money and hold Stellantis accountable for the commitments it made to our workers and our city,” the statement reads.
Unifor has previously written to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether Stellantis’ intentions to offload the plant breached its commitments to Ottawa.
Last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed disappointment over Stellantis moving Jeep Compass production to the United States.
At the time, the prime minister said he reminded Stellantis of its commitments to the government under funding deals — such as keeping the Brampton plant — and warned there would be consequences if it failed to meet those obligations.
Joly has said the government would “get our money back” if the company doesn’t fulfill its obligations. She said Monday that Stellantis’ decision “does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton.
“They deserve answers, respect and above all, a secure future,” Joly said in a statement.
The minister urged all parties to return to the bargaining table and said she has reached out to the automaker, union, Ontario government and representatives of the Brampton plant to convene a meeting this week.
“I expect them to come to the table with a single focus: protecting good paying jobs in Brampton,” Joly said.
“For Brampton’s autoworkers, walking away is not an option.”
Stellantis said it acknowledges its obligations to employees under collective agreements and applicable laws and that it “remains prepared to engage with Unifor to negotiate a settlement to assist union represented employees.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

Stellantis sells Canada plant to armored vehicle maker Roshel
sources.text:
[Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.]
Stellantis sells Canada plant to armored vehicle maker Roshel
Brampton plant's fate a prime example of effects of U.S. tariffs on Canada's auto sector
Bloomberg News
Key Takeaways:
- Stellantis signed a deal to sell its idled Brampton, Ontario, assembly plant to Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel for undisclosed terms.
- The plant once employed about 3,000 unionized workers, while Unifor argues the Roshel sale cannot replace lost auto assembly jobs.
- Stellantis expects the sale to close by year-end as Industry Minister Mélanie Joly seeks talks with Stellantis, Unifor and Ontario officials.
Stellantis NV signed a deal to sell an idled auto plant near Toronto to Roshel Inc., a Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer, for undisclosed terms.
The plant in Brampton, Ontario, once employed about 3,000 unionized workers but hasn’t been in production since late 2023, and has become a prime example of the damage to Canada’s auto sector caused by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” Antonio Filosa, Stellantis’ CEO, said in a statement, referring to the union that represents laid-off auto workers at the plant.
Stellantis was set to build the Jeep Compass SUV there, but scrapped that plan last year following Trump’s imposition of 25% tariffs on foreign-made cars. The automaker said those vehicles will be produced in Illinois instead.
Stellantis, created from the 2021 merger of Fiat Chrysler and France’s PSA Group, is grappling with stubbornly high U.S. inventory levels, persistent quality issues and fierce Chinese competition in Europe that have complicated turnaround efforts. To reignite growth, the automaker is in the midst of a turnaround effort and plans to spend some 60 billion euros ($67.2 billion) through 2030 to launch dozens of new models, prioritizing the Jeep, Ram, Peugeot and Fiat brands. In North America, it plans to add new trucks to try to rebuild sales.
But company executives have expressed significant doubts about whether the Brampton plant, which is about 40 years old, fits into those plans.
“Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers. Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of the national auto strategy,” says @Lanampayne on the sale of the Brampton Assembly Plant.
— Unifor (@UniforTheUnion) November 10, 2026
Roshel, whose head office is near the Brampton facility, is one of two finalists bidding on a Canadian military contract worth as much as C$4.9 billion ($3.5 billion) to build light utility vehicles, which would be manufactured at the plant.
Stellantis and Roshel signed a memorandum in September outlining the steps toward a sale. At that time, Roman Shimonov, Roshel’s chief executive officer, told Bloomberg News his firm would also work to attract other vehicle manufacturing and defense work to the plant.
“This proposal is not about creating a substitution to an automotive plant, but rather adding defense on top of the automotive production capabilities,” Shimonov said in September.
As part of its pitch for the Canadian military contract, Roshel has outlined partnerships with other Canadian firms, including the Algoma Steel Group Inc. mill in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. Last year, Roshel announced a partnership with Swedish steel producer Swebor Stal Svenska AB to establish Canada’s first facility entirely dedicated to producing ballistic-grade steel.
But the planned Roshel sale is staunchly opposed by Unifor.
“It’s clear that heavy corporate lobbying has convinced some in government that armoring trucks or reassembling cars is viable replacement work for Brampton,” Unifor National President Lana Payne posted on social media Nov. 7.
“Canada will have given up a lucrative auto assembly and supply chain capacity, for small batch, mostly contract-based upfitting work — turning tens of thousands of jobs into a few hundred.”
She reiterated her comments at a news conference on Nov. 8, adding that the Roshel deal “is not better.”
Bob Toews, CEO of TruckDown, discusses winter readiness in the connected fleet era. Tune in above or by going to RoadSigns.ttnews.com.
In its statement, Stellantis said it acknowledged its obligations to employees under the collective agreement and that it remains prepared to engage with Unifor.
It’s not immediately clear what say Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government would have over a sale transaction for the plant to a Canadian company — though it does control Roshel’s ability to get Canadian military contracts.
After Stellantis relocated the Jeep production line, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s department pursued legal action to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in financial help given to the company, alleging it had breached its commitments.
Stellantis spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin said Nov. 9 that the company has offered to voluntarily return the government support it received for the original retooling plan at the Brampton plant.
The company and government have not revealed how much federal money was provided to the firm, citing confidentiality agreements.
But a copy of the 2022 contract disclosed under access-to-information laws in Canada reveals that the federal government pledged up to C$529 million in funding for projects at both the Brampton plant and a facility in Windsor, Ontario.
Here is my statement on Stellantis: https://t.co/7JEvAUz6yr
— Mélanie Joly (@melaniejoly) November 9, 2026
Joly asked representatives from Unifor, Stellantis, the Ontario government and the Brampton plant to meet later this week, she said in a social media post.
“Stellantis’s decision does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton,” Joly said. “For Brampton’s auto workers, walking away is not an option.”
Stellantis said it expects the transaction to close by the end of 2026.

Stellantis Plant Sale 'best Thing That Can Happen' For Jobs And Brampton: Roshel CEO
sources.text:
Stellantis plant sale ‘best thing that can happen’ for jobs and Brampton: Roshel CEO
				November 10, 2026 
				
Roshel founder Roman Shimonov says the company is willing to hire back some of the 2,000 Stellantis employees who were laid off from the plant when it halted operations in 2023.
The chief executive of armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel is firing back at critics of his company’s deal to purchase the idled Stellantis plant in Brampton, Ont., defending it as “the best thing that can happen to this plant and to this city.”
Roshel founder Roman Shimonov says he’s surprised the government hasn’t publicly supported the sale given his company’s intention of creating thousands of jobs at the facility, and that he doesn’t “see any reason to be opposed to that.”
He says his Brampton-based company is willing to hire back some of the 2,000 Stellantis employees who were laid off from the plant when it halted operations in 2023.
Speaking at a news conference on the evening of Nov. 10, Unifor national president Lana Payne questioned why Roshel would choose the Brampton assembly plant and cast doubt that the defence contractor would need to hire as many workers that were employed there under Stellantis.
Stellantis announced the sale of the facility and associated equipment to Roshel for an undisclosed amount late afternoon on Nov. 10.
The companies say they expect the transaction to close by the end of this year, however it is subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.

sources.news_title: Stellantis Finally Sells Idled Brampton Plant, Canadian Defense Specialist Roshel Acquired It
sources.text:
Replacing a mass-production car factory with a defense contractor doesn't automatically restore historical production volumes, the previous headcount, or the supplier business that Brampton supported when it produced Dodge and Chrysler models there. Stellantis and Roshel have recently signed an asset purchase agreement covering the facility and its associated equipment.
Neither party has disclosed the purchase price, and the transaction does require government and regulatory approval. If everything goes according to plan, it should be completed by the end of 2026. Stellantis and Roshel are further exploring cooperation involving vehicle technologies and services tailored for the defense industry.
That being said, Brampton hasn't assembled a single road-going vehicle since December 2023. Its last hurrah included three familiar nameplates, beginning with the Chrysler 300 and mechanically similar Dodge Charger. The Challenger was also made there, for all three models featured mostly similar underpinnings and oily bits.
The final 300 rolled off the line on December 20 three years ago, whereas the last Charger and Challenger followed two days later. According to Dodge, the final units were a Destroyer Gray Scat Pack Widebody Charger and a Pitch Black SRT Demon 170 Challenger. The 300 had its own farewell earlier that month, with Chrysler bidding farewell to the full-size luxury sedan on December 8, 2023.
Unfortunately, this change of plans resulted in a Brampton workforce that remained on extended layoff. The prospect of a new vehicle program gradually disappeared, affecting nearby automotive suppliers in the process. Now that Roshel is calling the shots, the Canadian defense company needs additional manufacturing space.
Chief executive officer Roman Shimonov made it clear that the company had outgrown its existing manufacturing and research facilities, with Shimonov also highlighting that Roshel had produced more than 2,500 vehicles for Ukraine alone. Meaningful business, for sure, and it's even more so for a relatively young company. More specifically, Roshel Defence Solutions was founded in Toronto a decade ago, back in 2016.
A passenger vehicle assembly plant, however, depends on sustained production volumes and large workforces. Defense manufacturers may also need complex supply chains and skilled workers, but their output revolves around government or institutional procurement contracts. Otherwise put, Roshel isn't going to operate anything resembling the production system of Stellantis at the Brampton plant.
Speaking of Stellantis, the defense specialist intends to lease a quarter of the property back to Stellantis for automotive work. What kind of work? According to The Globe and Mail, that would be "possible vehicle assembly." It's easy to imagine a military version of the Ram HD or the Jeep Gladiator, but so far, nothing has been confirmed by either Stellantis or Roshel in this regard.

sources.text:
Stellantis Canada has confirmed the sale of its Brampton Assembly Plant.
The automaker announced on Monday afternoon that it has reached an asset purchase agreement with Canadian defence technology company Roshel for the facility and its contents.
Stellanis said that the sale is part of its FaSTLAne 2030 strategy, which is designed to enhance long-term competitiveness through "disciplined management of its manufacturing footprint."
Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa championed the move, while acknowledging the anxiety that it has caused Brampton plant workers.
"Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution," said Filosa. "With this announcement, we are driving forward our broader strategic goals, opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry, and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use."
The plant has been sitting idle for three years and has been a point of contention in the current contract talks between Stellantis and Unifor.
Unifor National President Lana Payne has condemned the announcement.
"Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to our members," said Payne in a statement. "Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of the national auto strategy and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect autoworkers in the U.S. trade war."
Payne added that before Monday's announcement, talks between Stellantis, the provincial and federal governments, and Unifor were being finalized.
In February, Brampton City Council unanimously voted to adjust bylaws to designate that Brampton Assembly was to be used as an auto assembly or manufacturing facility.
Unifor members voted 97.3 per cent in favour of strike action last month, and talks have been at an impasse since September. This also affects thousands of employees at the Windsor Assembly Plant.

sources.news_title: Stellantis finalizes sale of Brampton auto plant to defence contractor Roshel for undisclosed amount
sources.text:
Automaker Stellantis NV STLA-N says it has finalized the sale of its idled factory in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel Inc. for an undisclosed amount.
Stellantis closed the plant, which employed more than 3,000 people, for retooling in 2023, and moved planned production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois last year, after the U.S. imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars.
The deal is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory requirements, the companies said in a joint statement.
Honda, Ford show commitment to Canadian auto plants despite tariffs
Roshel’s owner, Roman Shimanov, said the Brampton plant could employ “thousands” of people, paying taxes and producing civilian and armoured vehicles.
“Every Canadian should be happy because we’re talking about a substantial change to a plant that was idle for three years,” he said by phone.
Unifor, which represents the workers, said the sale was a breach of the collective agreement and commitments to the federal government, which provided hundreds of millions of dollars to Stellantis to refit the plant.
“Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to our members,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said in a statement. “Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of the national auto strategy and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect autoworkers in the U.S. trade war.”
Ms. Payne called the sale “a significant step backwards for Canada’s industrial economy,” citing the loss of good Stellantis jobs and thousands more at parts suppliers.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement on X that she wants the automaker to meet with the Unifor union and provincial and federal officials this week to talk about “protecting good paying jobs in Brampton.”
“Stellantis’s decision does not erase the commitments they made to the workers of Brampton,” she said, adding that the government is focused on finding solutions for the more than 2,000 Stellantis workers who remain on layoff benefits.
“They deserve answers, respect and above all a secure future,” she said.
Ottawa has said Stellantis’s decision to shift production violated agreements the company made when it received taxpayer funding to retool the plant. Ms. Joly has said the government will get its money back.
Ottawa contributed as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor.
A source familiar with the matter told The Globe and Mail that Stellantis will lease back 25-per-cent of the plant for possible vehicle assembly while Roshel will retain control over the rest.
The Globe and Mail is not identifying the person because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.
The companies said in a statement that they will together pursue manufacturing opportunities for the massive factory northwest of Toronto.
Mr. Shimanov said it is too soon to talk about specific plans for the plant, but he has a letter of intent from a European carmaker that is interested in producing at the plant. That is in addition to the arrangement with Stellantis.
Roshel, which has plants in Mississauga, Brampton, Ohio, Mexico, France and Colombia, produced 1,500 armoured vehicles in 2025, he said. The company is among the bidders for the federal government’s light utility vehicle program, valued at about $5-billion.
From 2025: Laid off for years, Stellantis workers in Brampton confront a grim new reality
“You cannot sign a contract before you have the ability to produce,” Mr. Shimanov said. “It doesn’t work like that. You have to first have the capacity infrastructure before you commit to your clients. And our plan is first to secure the infrastructure. And then based on having the infrastructure, to offer different solutions, and this plan can offer a lot of different capabilities that are unique.”
Stellantis chief executive officer Antonio Filosa said the sale creates new opportunities in the defence business, “creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”
“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously,” he said. “After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution.”
Roshel is a Brampton-based maker of armoured vehicles for military and security industries.
Unifor has fought to reopen the plant, and walked away from collective bargaining talks with Stellantis in September when the employer confirmed it had a preliminary agreement to sell the facility, built in 1986. Before it closed in 2023, the plant made Dodge muscle cars.
The factory is 2.95 million square feet and sits on 269 acres.
Ottawa earlier rejected a Stellantis proposal to assemble Chinese car kits in the plant, dismissing it as a plan that would create few jobs and add little of value to the local supply chain.
Stellantis, maker of Fiat, Chrysler and several other global brands, has struggled to turn a profit and has excess capacity at its U.S. factories.

sources.news_title: Stellantis announces sale of Brampton assembly plant
sources.text: Stellantis has announced the sale of its Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defence technology company Roshel, a move that a union representing workers says amounts to a “betrayal.” In a news release issued late Monday afternoon, Stellantis and Roshel announced an agreement to sell the plant “for an undisclosed amount,” with the transaction expected to close by the end of this year. The sale, they said, will “create a path to return the Brampton Assembly Plant to productive industrial use.” More than 2,200 workers have been on layoff at the Brampton assembly plant since production was put on hold in December, 2023. “Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said in the release. “With this announcement, we are driving forward our broader strategic goals, opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.” ‘Stellantis has betrayed our members’ In a press conference Monday evening, Unifor President Lana Payne, said that the sale of the plant “has been and will be an unacceptable outcome for our union and our members.” “Selling an auto assembly plant and losing vehicle production capacity is devastating for the Canadian industry, for our country, but mostly for the workers who have given so much to this company over so many years. Because once that capacity is gone, it’s often gone for good,” Payne said. Payne described the sale as a “worst case scenario” and that Stellantis “has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers.” Payne called the sale a “continued breach” of the company’s commitments and said that “allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of our national auto strategy, and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect auto workers from this U.S. trade war.” “It’s really hard to believe this plant could have been sold without some green light from the federal government, Payne said.” Later in the press conference, Unifor Local President Vito Biato also condemmed the sale, and said that they told government officials that the move would “steer the auto industry down the wrong path.” “Some in government are hearing us, but just aren’t listening.” “Workers have done nothing but build the best cars for this company for decades. These same workers are now left chasing rumours. Stellantis has disrespected our members and our union. This is complete shameful and disgusting behaviour by Stellantis,” Biato said. Unifor officials said they had requested a meeting with Stellantis and government officials about the Brampton plant sale. In a statement, the union asked the City of Brampton and the Ontario government to “take all possible actions” to enforce bylaws which “explicitly designate the Brampton Assembly Plant location for automotive assembly.” Deal ends months of speculation In September, Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel for a potential sale of the plant, setting off months of speculation on its fate. On Monday, Roshel said that it plans to “create a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing” which will “allow Canadian companies to better serve customers at home and export into allied markets.” Roshel did not provide details on how many people would be employed at the facility, only saying that once complete it will “bring much-needed manufacturing space and jobs to the Toronto area.” In an interview with CTV News, Roshel CEO Roman Shimonoz said that his company plans to “maintain its purpose and to continue employing people under the automotive activity.” “We are looking and exploring different ways to ensure that we can create 1000s of jobs, and we’re doing that without waiting. And it’s very easy to criticise and be negative, but what is the alternative? This plant was idle for over three years. We now have a much better future, not just for people of this plant, but for Brampton, for Ontario, for Canada.” Stellantis received funding to retool plant In May, 2022 the federal government agreed to provide Stellantis with $529 million in funding to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants. In a statement, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the decision by Stellantis “does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton.” “We remain focused on finding solutions for the more than 2,000 affected workers and their families. They deserve answers, respect and, above all, a secure future,” Joly wrote. “All parties must come back to the bargaining table. I have reached out to representatives from Unifor, Stellantis, the Government of Ontario and the Brampton plant to convene a meeting later this week.” There is a long history of manufacturing at the Brampton assembly plant dating back to 1986. Most recently, the Dodge Charger and Dodge Challenger were assembled at the plant but the last of those vehicles rolled off the assembly line in 2023. At the time, Stellantis said that the plant would undergo improvements to begin manufacturing electric vehicles. In a statement, Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown reacted to the news saying that “the members of Unifor Local 1285 and their families have lived with years of uncertainty. They deserve a fair resolution from Stellantis and a clear path to good-paying jobs.” “I’m calling on Stellantis to work with Unifor to reach that resolution, and on Roshel to work directly with Local 1285 to identify hiring and training opportunities for laid-off Brampton autoworkers,” Brown said. “Stellantis must repay taxpayers for the public funding it received to support automotive production in Brampton. I will continue pressing the federal government to recover that money and hold Stellantis accountable for the commitments it made to our workers and our city.” Opposition leaders react In separate posts on X, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis blamed the federal Liberals and Prime Minister Mark Carney for failing to do enough to protect workers.

sources.news_title: Security Check
sources.text:
Stellantis says it has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.
Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the facility and associated equipment from the automaker for an undisclosed amount.
The companies said in a joint news release they are also exploring future collaboration opportunities across vehicle technologies and related services in the defence industry.
The move comes as contract talks between Stellantis and the union representing more than 9,000 of its workers in Canada remain at an impasse.
The two sides have clashed over the future of the Brampton site as well as issues around job security. Last month, Stellantis workers in Canada voted to give their union a mandate to strike, with 97.3 per cent of members in favour of authorizing a potential job action.
“We’re currently not in a strike position and obviously lots of this to be worked out. Our goal here is to reach a resolution and to get to the bargaining table when we can, and we’ll do our best to get an agreement,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said at a press conference Monday evening.
“A strike is always a last resort and it remains a last resort here.”
She said the union will evaluate its next move and that it has a “four-party meeting” scheduled for later in the week with the company and government officials to discuss the future of the Brampton plant.
Payne said the sale of an auto assembly plant and loss of vehicle production capacity is devastating for Canada’s industry.
“Having sold an auto plant is a worst-case scenario, and that’s what we’re facing right now. Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers,” she said.
“Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of our national auto strategy and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect autoworkers from this U.S. trade war.”
Talks broke down in September when Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel, a Brampton-based manufacturer of armoured vehicles, for a potential sale of the facility.
More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.
The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.
“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” said Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa in the news release.
“With this announcement, we are driving forward our broader strategic goals, opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry, and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”
Roshel founder and CEO Roman Shimonov said the company’s plan is to create a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing “which will allow Canadian companies to better serve customers at home and export into allied markets.”
“Aligned with Canada’s defence industrial strategy, it will strengthen our sovereign industrial capabilities, drive local economic growth and bring much-needed manufacturing space and jobs to the Toronto area,” Shimonov said in the release.
“We look forward to working collaboratively with government and the broader community to bring this vision to life.”
As the facility returns to operations, there will be opportunities for around 700 to 1,000 laid-off Stellantis employees to return to work under Roshel. The defence company also plans to lease around one-quarter of the site’s space back to Stellantis for automotive work.
The transaction is expected to close by the end of this year, subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.
Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown said in a statement Monday that he welcomes the opportunity for a local company to bring manufacturing back to the location.
He said Unifor members also deserve a fair resolution from Stellantis.
“I’m calling on Stellantis to work with Unifor to reach that resolution, and on Roshel to work directly with Local 1285 to identify hiring and training opportunities for laid-off Brampton autoworkers,” he said.
Brown said Stellantis also needs to repay taxpayers for the public funding it received to support automotive production in Brampton.
“I will continue pressing the federal government to recover that money and hold Stellantis accountable for the commitments it made to our workers and our city,” the statement reads.
Unifor has previously written to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether Stellantis’ intentions to offload the plant breached its commitments to Ottawa.
Last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed disappointment over Stellantis moving Jeep Compass production to the United States.
At the time, the prime minister said he reminded Stellantis of its commitments to the government under funding deals — such as keeping the Brampton plant — and warned there would be consequences if it failed to meet those obligations.
Joly has said the government would “get our money back” if the company doesn’t fulfil its obligations. She said Monday that Stellantis’ decision “does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton.”
“They deserve answers, respect and above all, a secure future,” Joly said in a statement.
The minister urged all parties to return to the bargaining table and said she has reached out to the automaker, union, Ontario government and representatives of the Brampton plant to convene a meeting this week.
“I expect them to come to the table with a single focus: protecting good paying jobs in Brampton,” Joly said.
“For Brampton’s autoworkers, walking away is not an option.”
Stellantis said it acknowledges its obligations to employees under collective agreements and applicable laws and that it “remains prepared to engage with Unifor to negotiate a settlement to assist union represented employees.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

sources.text:
Stellantis, corsa contro il tempo: oggi il vertice sulla vendita
TORONTO – È ancora scontro sulla vicenda legata alla decisione di Stellantis di vendere il suo stabilimento di Brampton. Se da un lato il sindacato dei metalmeccanici continua ad accusare l’azienda per il licenziamento di oltre 2.200 lavoratori e il governo per il suo presunto immobilismo, dall’altro è scattata la corsa contro il tempo per cercare di sciogliere la complicata matassa. È in programma per oggi il vertice che vedrà la presenza di tutte le parti in causa: rappresentanti dei due livelli di governo – Ottawa e Ontario – del sindacato Unifor, di Stellantis e di Roshel, la ditta canadese che produce veicoli militari e che è in fase d’acquisto dello stabilimento di Brampton.
Difficili, se non impossibile, trovare una soluzione che possa soddisfare tutti quanti. Stellantis, dal canto suo, ha giustificato la vendita per superare l’impasse che dura ormai da tre anni nello stabilimento di Brampton e non sembra intenzionata a tornare sui propri passi.
Il governo federale continua a chiedere a gran voce il rispetto degli impegni presi in precedenza – che in linea teorica garantivano la continuità della produzione – alla luce anche dei sostanziosi incentivi e stanziamenti fatti negli ultimi anni per convincere il gigante dell’auto a rimanere a Brampton. E proprio su questo punto potrebbe aprirsi un ulteriore fronte, visto che dati alla mano Ottawa nel 2022 ha elargito a Stellantis 529 milioni di dollari per i due stabilimenti di Brampton e Windsor, soldi che ovviamente l’esecutivo vuole riavere. Ma la compagnia sarebbe disposta a restituire solamente 24 milioni di dollari.
A complicare ulteriormente la vicenda sono state pubblicate ieri delle rivelazioni esplosive che se fossero confermate renderebbero molto scomoda la posizione dell’esecutivo.
Secondo Ctv, infatti, rappresentanti del governo guidato da Mark Carney sarebbero stati presenti in numerosi incontri nei quali sarebbe stata discussa la vendita dello stabilimento a Roshel: secondo le fonti sentite da Ctv, il governo federale non si sarebbe mai opposto alla decisione di Stellantis di vendere e non avrebbe sollevato obiezioni dopo la presentazione dell’offerta di Roshel. Una posizione, quella che emerge in questo retroscena che tuttavia deve essere confermato, che stride fortemente con le dichiarazioni ufficiali dello stesso primo ministro e della ministra del Lavoro Melanie Joly, che hanno accusato Stellantis di “aver tradito i lavoratori di Brampton e gli accordi siglati con il governo”.
Ora resta appeso a un filo il destino delle migliaia di operai che hanno perso il posto di lavoro. Roshel ha già fatto sapere che sulla eventuale riassunzione non ci saranno garanzie.
In alto, lo stabilimento di Brampton (foto: Unifor)

sources.news_title: NDP: Brampton Stellantis sale should be a wake-up call for Doug Ford
sources.text:
November 10th, 2026
WINDSOR WEST — Following Stellantis' announcement about the sale of the Brampton assembly plant, the Leader of the Official Opposition Marit Stiles; Shadow Minister for the Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services, Lisa Gretzky (Windsor West); and Shadow Minister for Labour, Jamie West (Sudbury) released the following statement:
"Stellantis made commitments to Brampton, in writing, and has spent the last year breaking them. This should be a wake-up call for Doug Ford,” said Stiles.
“Ontario could be losing good, union jobs in a key sector in the middle of a trade war. Doug Ford needs to fight for Ontario’s auto workers and the future of this sector. This is devastating for thousands of workers and their families, and it tells us once again that Doug Ford has no plan to protect Ontario’s autoworkers.”
"Workers in Windsor are worried that their jobs are next on the chopping block, since Doug Ford and his government have made it very clear that there are no consequences for companies that don't follow through on commitments they've made to workers and the communities they live in,” said MPP Gretzky.
"Leaving workers and residents in a state of fear over immense job losses is not leadership: it's blatant neglect of Ontario workers amidst an ongoing trade war and cost of living crisis. Workers deserve to see their governments fighting like hell for their jobs, which includes holding companies accountable for not honouring agreements."
"Ford is failing to protect good union jobs during this trade war," said MPP West. "He's shown time and time again, first with Stelco and now with Stellantis, that his priority is not to look out for Ontario workers. Ford and his Conservatives need to stand up for Ontario workers."

sources.news_title: Stellantis Sells Brampton After $1B Subsidy Dispute, New Owner Rejects Worker Obligations
sources.text:
Roshel’s proposed revival of Stellantis’ Brampton assembly plant now includes an unnamed major European automaker interested in Canadian production, but the prospective partnership comes without a finalized manufacturing contract or commitments to preserve the jobs and benefits of more than 2,200 displaced workers.
Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov disclosed during a CBC interview that the company had received a letter of intent from a European original equipment manufacturer seeking to establish vehicle production in Brampton.
Shimonov said Roshel had shared the document with the federal government, although the automaker’s identity and proposed production arrangements remain undisclosed.
He acknowledged that the letter does not constitute a finalized agreement. Securing a firm production commitment would require Roshel to complete its acquisition and gain control of the facility.
The announcement introduces a potential alternative to the loss of conventional automotive assembly at Brampton, where Stellantis previously planned to manufacture the Jeep Compass before transferring production to Illinois.
Shimonov maintained that Roshel intends to retain the plant’s automotive manufacturing capabilities, producing civilian vehicles alongside defence equipment.
Thousands of jobs while excluding worker obligations
The company’s longer-term ambitions extend beyond the 700 to 1,000 potential employment opportunities for displaced Stellantis workers previously reported by The Canadian Press.
Shimonov said Roshel aims to employ thousands of people across its proposed manufacturing operations, prioritizing Brampton residents. However, he explicitly stated that Roshel would not assume Stellantis’ previous obligations to employees.
“We’re not taking over responsibilities or obligations that Stellantis made in the past,” Shimonov said, speaking to Ian Hanomansing on CBC’s Hanomansing Live.
He also declined to specify whether future Roshel employees would receive compensation and benefits comparable to those under Stellantis’ collective agreement.
Roshel’s larger employment ambitions predate the acquisition. In July, Shimonov discussed creating thousands of jobs if the company secured a major Canadian military vehicle procurement contract.
$1.04 billion subsidy dispute remains
The ownership transition also leaves unresolved the government’s financial dispute with Stellantis. Ottawa and Ontario committed up to $1.042 billion in 2022 to support the automaker’s combined Windsor and Brampton modernization program.
Federal records show approximately $222.4 million had been disbursed across the two facilities by March 31, 2025. Ottawa subsequently suspended further payments following Stellantis’ decision to move Jeep production to the United States.
The federal government issued Stellantis a formal notice of default in December 2025. The amount potentially recoverable remains undisclosed.
Unifor condemned the sale on Monday, alleging that Stellantis breached its labour and government commitments. Stellantis says it remains prepared to negotiate a settlement with Unifor.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly maintained that selling Brampton does not eliminate Stellantis’ responsibilities to affected workers.
Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the plant and equipment for an undisclosed amount, with closing expected before year-end. The Canadian Press also reported plans for Stellantis to lease approximately one-quarter of the facility for automotive activities.
In September, Joly said Ottawa is applying “maximum pressure” on the automaker to commit a new model to the site.

sources.news_title: Stellantis sells Brampton plant to Canadian defense manufacturer Roshel
sources.text:
On the Dash:
- Stellantis signed an agreement to sell its idled Brampton Assembly Plant and related equipment to Roshel for an undisclosed amount. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals.
- Roshel plans to turn the facility into a Centre of Excellence for advanced manufacturing, with the goal of supporting Canadian defense production and exports to allied markets.
- Unifor criticized the sale as a breach of Stellantis’ commitments to its workers, while Stellantis said it remains prepared to negotiate a settlement with the union.
Stellantis announced Monday that it signed an Asset Purchase Agreement to sell its idled Brampton Assembly Plant in Ontario and associated equipment to Roshel, a Canadian defense technology company, in a deal the two companies expect to close by the end of 2026, pending fulfillment of closing conditions and necessary government and regulatory approvals.
The companies didn’t disclose the purchase price but also established a strategic cooperation framework to explore global collaboration on vehicle technologies and related defense-industry services. Stellantis said the agreement creates an opportunity to return the idle facility to productive industrial use while supporting Roshel’s growth and potential joint business opportunities.
While Roshel plans to establish a Centre of Excellence for advanced manufacturing at the Brampton facility, Roshel Founder and CEO Roman Shimonov said it would help Canadian companies serve domestic customers and export products to allied markets while aligning with Canada’s Defence Industrial Strategy, strengthening domestic industrial capabilities, supporting local economic growth and creating manufacturing jobs in the Toronto area. In the company’s media release, he said, “We look forward to working collaboratively with government and the broader community to bring this vision to life.”
Unifor, the union representing the plant’s workers, questioned whether those job commitments would materialize, and Local 1285 President Vito Beato said procurement contracts to fill the plant haven’t been secured yet.
Unifor calls sale a betrayal
The sale arrives amid ongoing negotiations between Stellantis and Unifor, which represents the plant’s workforce. The previous contract expired Sept. 20 after talks reached an impasse in September, and workers voted Oct. 17 and 18 to authorize a strike after Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel on a potential sale.
Unifor said it had been working toward four-party talks involving Stellantis, the union and both the Ontario and Canadian governments on the automaker’s future manufacturing plans in Canada, and Unifor National President Lana Payne called the sale a betrayal of workers that the union said violates the collective agreement and breaks commitments Stellantis made to the Canadian government. Payne also warned the sale could lead to further job losses among suppliers.
Meanwhile, Brampton City Council voted in February to amend zoning bylaws designating the property for automotive assembly and related manufacturing, and Unifor is urging local and provincial officials to enforce it. Notbaly, the sale would affect roughly 2,200 Unifor members.
For its part, Stellantis said the sale aligns with its FaSTLAne 2030 strategy, which calls for disciplined management of its manufacturing footprint and approximately 80% capacity utilization across North America by 2030. Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa emphasized the company’s commitment to Brampton employees after three years of paid layoffs, and the company said it will work with Unifor on a fair resolution and is ready to negotiate a settlement for union-represented employees. Stellantis added that the defense partnership could open new opportunities as the U.S. government has approached domestic automakers about supporting military manufacturing, munitions production and vehicle supply chains.

Written by The Canadian Press on November 9, 2026
BRAMPTON — Stellantis says it has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.
Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the facility and associated equipment from the automaker for an undisclosed amount.
More coming.
